Motivation.after: Second, joint friction prevents us from achieving perfect alignment between the grinding tool and the configured plane.
Motivation.note: Suggested wording: friction can contribute to the difference between desired and achieved orientation. These experiments do not isolate friction as the sole cause.

Motivation.after: The idea is to use impedance control, which, unlike conventional rigid control, allows the tool to respond to external forces and moments by making rotation compliant, for example.
Motivation.note: More precise: compare this with stiff position control. Conventional control is not always rigid.
Suggested wording: contact moments rotate the tool towards alignment. Complete physical flatness is not established by the recorded angular-error component.

Cartesian impedance controller.note: Clarification: translation and rotation are decoupled in this impedance law before shifting the reference point. This does not mean the robot dynamics or physical contact are completely uncoupled.

Translation–rotation coupling.note: Clarification: the CoC is a virtual reference for the entire impedance model. Moving it does not move the physical contact point.
Correction: define stiffness and damping at the CoC, then transform them to the TCP. The resulting TCP matrices have off-diagonal blocks that couple translation and rotation.

Contact experiment.note: Suggested wording: the tool rotates towards alignment during contact establishment. Perfect flatness is not guaranteed, and the reported experiments evaluate this five-second phase rather than grinding performance.

Angular quantities.note: More precise: the plots use the angular-error component about the first surface tangent, calculated from the tool normal and calibrated surface normal. The measured angular offset is its value at contact entry.

Normal-force plausibility assessment.note: Correction: state the stiffness unit as N/m. The measured error change is −19.65 mm, giving a quasi-static prediction of −19.65 N.
Clarification: compare means in the shaded stationary interval. The estimate differs from the command by 13.50% and comes from the robot model, not an independent force sensor.

Moment plausibility assessment.note: Correction: use approximately 6.57 degrees and a stiffness of 15 N m/rad. Convert the angle to radians to obtain approximately 1.72 N m.
Suggested wording: these tests support the plausibility of the implemented impedance relations. Agreement in two quasi-static tests does not prove the entire controller correct.

Commanded and estimated wrench.note: Correction: the model estimate is available before motion. Friction can affect motion onset and estimation, but this plot alone does not identify the cause of the initial behaviour.
Suggested wording: a change is visible near 0.4 seconds, followed by changing force and moment. Identifying first contact requires an event reference, and the moment is not linear throughout.

Commanded and estimated wrench.after: Once the tool is flat, the force and moment become stationary, and the measurement is exactly equal to the command.
Commanded and estimated wrench.note: Correction: say stationary contact and close agreement. The stationary mean differences are 2.32% for force and 4.87% for moment, and this plot does not establish perfect flatness.
Suggested wording: this is consistent with contact-driven rotation while the desired orientation remains fixed. The gap between commanded and estimated moments alone does not prove passive alignment.

Baseline angular error.after: Next, this plot shows the final angular error for three different starting orientations: 0, +10 and −10 degrees.
Baseline angular error.note: Clarification: those are nominal commands. The measured entry offsets are 0.69, +9.31 and −9.41 degrees, with final errors of 1.65, 1.75 and 1.41 degrees.
Suggested wording: the two entry directions give different errors. Friction, calibration and tool-mount uncertainty may contribute, but the experiments do not separate their individual effects.

Effect of rotational stiffness.note: Correction: the error increases from 1.75 to 6.58 degrees, approximately 3.76 times, or nearly four times. Rotational stiffness is measured in N m/rad.

Effect of CoC position.note: Clarification: +10 and −10 degrees are nominal starting commands. The plotted conditions have measured entry tilts of approximately +9.32 and −9.36 degrees.
Correction: the error magnitude continues improving from 1.41 degrees at 0 mm to 0.94 degrees at +10 mm, then worsens. A residual error of about 2 degrees does not establish perfect flatness.
Correction: positive-entry error is already 8.33 degrees at −20 mm, versus 1.89 degrees at −10 mm. The tested points show a sharp change between them, not a universal 20 mm threshold.

Angular error and interaction wrench.note: Correction: say little correction at −40 mm. The 2.5 versus 3.6 seconds compares settling within 0.1 degree of each trace’s own endpoint, not the time to become flat.
Correction: the stationary forces are similar, approximately −83, −79 and −78 N. A lower transient in one representative trial does not establish a generally lower required pressing force.

Suggested wording: the opposing configuration has a somewhat larger force magnitude here. Attributing this specifically to end-effector position requires checking the recorded position error and transformed impedance terms.

Correction: the quantified one-second improvement concerns angular-error settling. The final errors are about 1.75 degrees at the TCP and 1.49 degrees at +40 mm, so complete flatness is not demonstrated.
Correction: the estimated TCP moments change direction, with stationary values about +4.07, +0.73 and −2.54 N m at −40, 0 and +40 mm. The supporting case does not simply require less contact moment.

Null-space controller.note: Clarification: one null-space direction exists when the Jacobian has full row rank. It combines motions of several joints and gives zero instantaneous end-effector velocity.
Suggested wording: regulate unwanted redundant motion. Damping suppresses motion, while conditioning deliberately moves along the null space to improve local conditioning.
More precise: at a singularity, an instantaneous motion direction is lost. Near a singularity, achieving some end-effector velocities requires very large joint velocities.

Null-space experiment.note: Correction: this is a virtual 20 N point force on link three, implemented as joint torques through its point Jacobian. Joint one receives the largest equivalent disturbance torque, not the only torque.

Cumulative joint motion.note: Correction: cumulative joint motion accumulates the magnitude of projected motion using all seven joint velocities. It is not the absolute angle travelled by the disturbed joint alone.

Jacobian conditioning.note: Suggested wording: conditioning alone and combined control keep the minimum singular value nearly constant. The small difference in their absolute levels does not establish that combined control improves conditioning more.

Joint motion over time.note: Clarification: this plot shows the measured joint-one angle relative to disturbance onset. The earlier cumulative metric describes projected motion across all seven joints.
Suggested wording: adding damping reduces cumulative motion, but reversals remain. A smoother response is not established by the cumulative-motion reduction alone.

Conclusion.note: Suggested wording: compliant rotation allowed contact moments to reduce angular error. Residual errors and calibration uncertainty remain, so say towards alignment rather than completely flat.
